query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating enhanced free-energy sampling methods (such as interface pinning or metadynamics) with machine-learned interatomic potentials specifically trained for multi-principal-element systems can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline high-entropy alloys near their melting point under high-temperature equilibrium conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply an advanced free-energy method that couples enhanced sampling (e.g., interface pinning/metadynamics) with ML-driven interatomic potentials tailored for HEAs.
generation.conditions: High-temperature equilibrium conditions at phase coexistence, with the alloys spanning the compositional space typical of HEAs (5 or more elements in roughly 5–35% atomic fractions).
generation.structural_mediator: The free-energy sampling technique elucidates the free-energy barrier between solid and liquid phases, while the ML potentials accurately capture complex interatomic forces in multicomponent systems.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling methods rigorously converge free-energy differences at the melting transition, resolving subtle latent heat and volume changes. ML-trained potentials achieve computational efficiency and accuracy over the vast compositional space by precisely parameterizing interatomic interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperatures predicted with an error margin under ±30 K and fusion enthalpy/entropy values within a few percent error; accurate estimation of volume change at melting and liquid-phase properties across diverse HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Traditional techniques (e.g., DSC, CALPHAD, standard atomistic simulations) that offer lower resolution and suffer from high computational cost when extended across the compositional complexity of HEAs.
generation.boundary: Applicable to high-entropy alloys with multiple principal elements under near-equilibrium, high-temperature conditions. Systems with excessive compositional inhomogeneity or non-equilibrium behavior may fall outside the method’s effective range.
generation.uncertainty: Potential uncertainties include the accuracy and transferability of the ML potentials for all HEA compositions, as well as possible convergence challenges in free-energy sampling of highly disordered liquid phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the integrated free-energy sampling and ML potential method to a well-characterized HEA (e.g., HEA WTaMoNbV) and compare the predicted melting temperature and fusion properties to high-accuracy experimental data obtained from advanced calorimetric techniques.
measurements: Melting temperature with a tolerance of ±30 K
Fusion enthalpy and entropy within a few percent deviation
Volume change at melting measured via independent high-temperature dilatometry or X-ray/neutron imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted melting temperature and fusion thermodynamic properties deviate from the experimental measurements beyond the target error margins in multiple HEA compositions, then the proposed method is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. frame.goal: To determine key melting-related thermodynamic properties — melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties — with both high accuracy and efficiency across a wide compositional space.

decision.trend: In the earlier studies on high‐entropy alloys, researchers initially relied on standard experimental probes (e.g., calorimetry, DSC) and conventional computational approaches (such as CALPHAD and routine atomistic simulations) to extract thermophysical and phase‐stability data. Some works even used additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., selective laser melting and LPBF) that inherently involve melting and rapid solidification, while concurrently comparing experimental measurements with CALPHAD predictions. These efforts provided valuable insights into phase formation and high‐temperature behavior but have not been extended to reliably capture the complete free energy landscape associated with melting (including latent heat and subtle volume changes) over the vast compositional space of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: The challenge that remains is to obtain both high accuracy and computational efficiency when determining key fusion thermodynamic properties (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change, and liquid-phase properties) for complex multicomponent, high-entropy systems. In particular, existing techniques do not sufficiently address the difficulty in resolving the free energy barrier at melting transitions across diverse compositions with a method that is both broadly applicable and decisively benchmarked.
decision.lever: Integrate advanced free-energy methods—such as interface pinning or metadynamics—with machine-learned interatomic potentials that are explicitly parameterized for the multi-principal-element systems found in HEAs. Key parameters would include precise control over phase coexistence conditions, rigorous convergence of free energy differences at the melting transition (error margins in the melting temperature below ~30 K and enthalpy/entropy errors within a few percent), and robust sampling across the compositional space.
decision.why: This approach naturally follows from the trend of moving beyond standard calorimetric and conventional simulation methods by directly targeting the free-energy landscape. By coupling enhanced sampling techniques with accurate, computationally efficient ML-driven potentials, the method is tailored to meet the stringent accuracy and efficiency targets of melting-property determination for high-entropy alloys. It also offers a decisive validation: a systematic mismatch between predicted and experimentally measured fusion thermodynamics for a well‐characterized composition would rule out the approach.
